extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of comic fiction; students of P.G. Wodehouse's style
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and describe the comedic techniques exemplified in this excerpt of P.G. Wodehouse (Archie/George/Albert scenes) to guide humor writing or analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narratorial ironic asides / authorial intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The omniscient narrator interrupts the action with wry commentary and judgments (e.g., 'There is probably no attitude of mind harder for the average man to maintain than that of aloof disapproval.'; 'That is Life. Just one long succession of misunderstandings...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a conversational, mildly sardonic narrator who comments on characters and events to add an extra comic layer; short aphoristic sentences and hyperbolic generalizations work well. Avoid letting asides derail the scene's forward motion — keep them punchy and relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-contrast comedy (social inversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy arises from contrasts between characters' social stations and behavior (e.g., a gentleman waiter, a precocious page-boy who 'knows the ropes', and silly, upper-class suitors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit mismatches between expected role and behavior (servants clever, masters foolish) to create ironic situations; maintain clear, distinct roles so the inversion is visible. Don't make contrasts vague — the sharper the mismatch, the stronger the comic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialect and distinctive speech patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is generated by vividly rendered spoken voices, such as Albert's clipped, phonetic working-class speech ('Wri'!', 'I 'ave a scheme', 'sweepstike').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give minor characters strong, consistent verbal quirks (misspellings, contractions, phonetic renderings) to produce comedic texture and economy of characterization. Use sparingly to avoid obscuring meaning or alienating readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malapropism / phonetic mis-hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic effect from mistaken or comically spelled words (example: 'sweepstike' for sweepstake; repeated 'ginger-ile' variants), and characters misunderstanding each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce near-misses and mis-hearings to generate gentle farce; ensure context makes the intended word clear so the joke rests on the mistake rather than confusion. Avoid piling similar errors in one scene that would reduce clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and running motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of words/phrases for comic emphasis (e.g., 'Hey, mister!' recurs; 'Kitty, Kitty, Kitty!' followed by Albert's derisive reaction), and callbacks later in action (knotted sheet later attributed to Reggie).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition to build expectation and then subvert it or escalate the joke; callbacks reward attentive readers. Don't overuse repetition — it should escalate or reveal something new on repeat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggerated simile and hyperbole
rubrics_metrics.description: Large, absurd comparisons and overstatement produce comic imagery (e.g., 'Wings seemed to sprout from Reggie's shapely shoulders'; dress 'made of rose-leaves and moon-beams'; 'a half-brick... must infallibly have spilt blue blood').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ vivid, improbable metaphors to heighten comedy and character reaction. Balance the extravagance with straight narration so the hyperbole stands out; avoid metaphors so outlandish they break immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational irony and misunderstandings driving plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor and plot both come from misapprehensions and near-misses (George hidden on balcony overhears Plummer's proposal; servants' sweepstake makes Lady Maud a 'prize').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure scenes so misunderstandings create escalating complications that produce both comedy and narrative momentum. Ensure stakes are clear so the audience cares about the resulting absurdities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical comedy / staged pratfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical embarrassment and risky business (balcony escape, knotted-sheet descent) are used for comedic suspense and payoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical peril played as comic — plausible yet sufficiently improbable to be funny; time descriptions to maximize tension and release. Keep physical comedy coherent and describable to avoid confusion about what happens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing and timing (pauses, interruptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent interruptions and pauses ('Hey, mister!' interjections, Albert's intrusions) create comic beats and break romantic or serious moments for humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose dialogue and beats so pauses/interruptions break expectations at the right moment; use short sentences or single-word interrupts to punctuate timing. Avoid disrupting necessary exposition — choose beats that add humor without derailing comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understatement and anti-climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Downplaying dramatic feelings or events for comic contrast (George's shy, halting responses to love; laconic summaries of chaos: 'It was an awful row! Shoutin' and yellin' and cussin' all over the shop.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver large events with flat, underplayed commentary to create irony. Use understatement to let the reader supply the comedic contrast; avoid making the understatement so subtle it goes unnoticed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogic rhythm and economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Short, clipped exchanges and mismatched registers (formal 'sir' from George in waiter role vs. casual banter) generate comedy and reveal character swiftly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write dialogue with distinct cadences for each character; use economy — a few well-placed lines can accomplish characterization and joke simultaneously. Steer clear of long monologues that slow comic tempo unless deliberately used for contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalation from small detail to larger farce
rubrics_metrics.description: A minor servant gossip (sweepstake) becomes a significant plot point affecting romantic prospects, turning a small jest into major complication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seed small, odd details early that can pay off later as complications; escalate stakes logically from the tiny absurdity so the farce feels inevitable. Avoid planting too many red herrings that never resolve.
